prompt: Match each skill to its group on the map.

pairs.left: Knowing what a gross margin is
Putting the finding in the first line of an email

prompt: By the lesson, what happens to an analyst who knows every tool but cannot say how the company makes money?

choices.text: Builds accurate dashboards about the wrong things
choices.why: Right: the business group is what points the tools at questions that matter.

choices.text: Produces numbers that are wrong more often than other analysts' numbers
choices.why: The numbers can be perfectly right; the lesson's point is what they are about.

choices.text: Becomes a data engineer instead
choices.why: Roles are defined by what is delivered, not by what an analyst lacks.

choices.text: Is fine, since the business is the managers' job and not the analyst's
choices.why: The lesson calls the business group the one that separates a useful answer from a correct one.

prompt: What test does the lesson give for whether an analyst knows a skill "at a working level"?

choices.text: Holding a certificate in it
choices.why: The lesson's test is about the work, not about paper.

choices.text: Being the best in the company at it
choices.why: The lesson says explicitly that is not needed.

choices.text: Whether its absence would stop a piece of work
choices.why: Right: not writing a join means waiting for somebody; not knowing a margin means not checking a finance report.

choices.text: Having used it every day for at least a year in a previous job
choices.why: Time spent is not the test; Lívia learned the monthly close in her first month.

prompt: What share of Varanda's 2025 sales did December make, in percent to one decimal?
In your sheet, what share of Lívia's 176 hours went on building dashboards and charts, in percent to one decimal?
Answering requests took 36 hours and meetings with the business 37. What share of the 176 hours is that together, in percent to one decimal?
The shares in Lívia's sheet add up to exactly 100, while the shares in lesson 1 added up to 99.9. What does the lesson say about the difference?
hint: Each share is rounded on its own.

choices.text: Lesson 1's sheet had a mistake that this one fixed
choices.why: Lesson 1 called its 99.9 honest; there was no mistake.

choices.text: This sheet rounds the total, which the first one did not
choices.why: Both round each share and neither rounds the total.

choices.text: Luck: both sums are honest
choices.why: Right: the roundings happened to cancel this time; whether separate roundings cancel is luck, not quality.

choices.text: A sum of 100 proves every share in the column is right
choices.why: A sum of 100 is consistent with a wrong share elsewhere; it proves nothing about each one.

prompt: Helena reads Lívia's log and concludes that BI is mostly overhead, since only 9.1% of the hours produced a dashboard. What does the lesson reply?
hint: The last step of work that mostly happened before it.

choices.text: That Lívia should spend more time on dashboards next month
choices.why: More charts without the work behind them is the report factory of lesson 1.

choices.text: That the other hours are what make the charts worth trusting
choices.why: Right: requests find the question, checks make the number right, definitions keep it the same.

choices.text: That the log is wrong, because analysts spend most of their time building
choices.why: The log adds up to a full working month and the lesson takes it at face value.

choices.text: That dashboards are not part of BI at all
choices.why: They are part of it; they are the last and smallest part of the hours.

prompt: Put the five questions for taking a request in the order the lesson asks them.
items: What will you decide with this?
trap: Starting from the definition feels technical and safe, but without the decision nobody knows which number to define.

prompt: Which of the five questions does the lesson say turns a vague request into a measurable one?
hint: It names the result that matters before anybody sees the data.

choices.text: Who decides?
choices.why: That sets the audience and the form, not what would be measured.

choices.text: By when?
choices.why: That sets the deadline.

choices.text: What would change your mind?
choices.why: Right: it fixes in advance the result that would change the action — Renata's R$ 10 an order.

choices.text: Which tool?
choices.why: That is not one of the five; the tool comes after the question.

prompt: Renata asked for a sales dashboard with "everything". What did the five questions turn it into?

choices.text: A larger dashboard with every channel and region, delivered a week later
choices.why: The questions narrowed the request; they did not widen it.

choices.text: One table and one chart, by channel and month
choices.why: Right: cost per order, paid search against email, shaped by the decision to keep or cut paid search before 31 March.

choices.text: A refusal, since there was no decision behind it
choices.why: There was a decision; the questions found it.

choices.text: A model predicting next month's orders
choices.why: Nothing in the conversation asked for a prediction.

prompt: When somebody only wants to "keep an eye on" a number, the lesson changes the question to "what would make you act?", and the answer is a ___.
hint: A level that, once crossed, calls for action.

prompt: The agency counts paid-search orders by last click; Renata's team counts the first channel that brought the customer. What did Lívia and Renata agree to do?

choices.text: Use the agency's figure, since the agency measures the campaign
choices.why: The agency is paid by the campaign, which is a reason to show its figure beside another, not alone.

choices.text: Average the two counts into one
choices.why: An average of two definitions is a third definition nobody chose.

choices.text: Use Renata's figure and drop the agency's
choices.why: They kept both; dropping one would hide how much the answer depends on the choice.

choices.text: Write both definitions down and show both, side by side
choices.why: Right: the decision can then be checked against each.

prompt: Lívia's Monday check found Betim's file empty. What went out?
hint: A missing number said out loud.

choices.text: Nothing; the email waited until the file was fixed
choices.why: The email went out on time, with the gap stated.

choices.text: The email, with a line saying Betim's figure was missing
choices.why: Right: better than a total about R$ 170,000 short that nobody would question.

choices.text: The email, with Betim's figure copied from the week before
choices.why: Filling a gap with an old number presents a guess as a measurement.

choices.text: The email, with the total for the eight stores that sent files
choices.why: Without a note, that total is about R$ 170,000 short and looks complete.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson count among the analyst's responsibilities? Choose all that apply.
hint: Six things no request will ask for.

choices.text: Keeping the written definition of every published number
choices.why: Right: the owner decides; the analyst makes sure it is written and the same everywhere.

choices.text: Saying "we don't know yet" when the data cannot settle a question
choices.why: Right: a confident answer the data cannot back is acted on.

choices.text: Deciding what each number means
choices.why: That is the owner's; the analyst keeps it written down.

choices.text: Showing salaries by band rather than by name
choices.why: Right: a report shows what its reader needs and no more.

choices.text: Matching the figure the director expected
choices.why: That is the one thing the lesson says never to do.

prompt: Renata asks whether the paid-search figures could leave out the two weeks the campaign was paused. What does the lesson present as the right response?

choices.text: Refuse, since any change to a period is manipulation
choices.why: Looking again is fine; hiding a version is the problem.

choices.text: Agree, since Renata owns the number
choices.why: Owning a definition is deciding it in advance, not changing it when the result disappoints.

choices.text: Show both versions, labelled, and say which answers the agreed question
choices.why: Right: nothing is hidden, and the agreed question decides which is the answer.

choices.text: Show the version that leaves the weeks out, with a footnote
choices.why: That leads with the convenient version; the lesson shows both and names the answer.

prompt: The lesson's test for documentation is whether somebody else could ___ the work next year and get the same answer without asking you.
Caio emails: "Can you send me deliveries by region for the last two years?" What should Lívia do first, by this lesson?
hint: The request is a guess at what would help.

choices.text: Export the two years and send them the same day
choices.why: Fast, and possibly useless: nobody knows yet what it is for.

choices.text: Build a dashboard of deliveries by region so he can explore
choices.why: That is a bigger version of the same guess.

choices.text: Ask what he will decide with it, and by when
choices.why: Right: the first questions find the decision that shapes everything else.

choices.text: Ask Helena whether Caio's request should be done
choices.why: The analyst can find out what the request is for without escalating it.

prompt: Match each of Lívia's actions to the responsibility it carries out.
hint: Six responsibilities; four of them here.

pairs.left: A link to the definition of a sale at the foot of the Monday email
Comparing the total with the finance system's daily takings
Writing down where the repeat rate's data came from and what was left out
Showing headcount costs by salary band

prompt: A new analyst spends her first month building twelve dashboards and logs almost no hours on requests, checks or definitions. By this lesson, what is the likeliest problem?
hint: Compare with where Lívia's hours went.

choices.text: She is too slow at building, since twelve is few for a month
choices.why: Speed of building is not the issue the lesson raises.

choices.text: The dashboards answer no known decision and rest on unchecked numbers
choices.why: Right: without the requests and the checks, the charts are the report factory of lesson 1.

choices.text: Nothing: dashboards are the visible part of BI and she produced plenty
choices.why: Visible output is what the lesson warns against counting.

choices.text: She should have used a different BI tool
choices.why: The tool is not the issue anywhere in this lesson.
